A 5-day-old term newborn who has been exclusively breastfed is brought to the emergency department for vomiting and decreased urine output.  Vital signs show tachycardia and hypotension.  Physical examination shows a lethargic, jaundiced newborn with a sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, and hepatomegaly.  Laboratory studies show leukocytosis with a left shift, hypoglycemia, and elevated transaminases.  Intravenous fluids, dextrose, and empiric antibiotics are administered.  Preliminary blood culture results show gram-negative rods.  Breastfeeding is discontinued, and a special formula is initiated.  The patient's condition gradually improves over the next few days.  Which of the following steps in metabolism is most likely impaired in this patient?

 
​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​
explanation:
This neonate with vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and hypoglycemia most likely has classic galactosemia, an autosomal recessive disorder caused by galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) deficiency.

Lactose, the principal carbohydrate in breast milk, is hydrolyzed by intestinal lactase to glucose and galactose.  Galactokinase phosphorylates galactose to galactose-1-phosphate.  GALT then catalyzes the following reaction:

Galactose-1-phosphate + UDP-glucose ⇌ UDP-galactose + glucose-1-phosphate

UDP-galactose can be epimerized to regenerate UDP-glucose, and glucose-1-phosphate can be converted to glucose-6-phosphate for use in glycolysis.

In classic galactosemia, absent or markedly reduced GALT activity causes galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, which contributes to hepatic and renal toxicity.  Symptoms typically develop within days of starting breast milk or lactose-containing formula.  Vomiting and poor feeding cause dehydration, whereas impaired hepatic metabolism and reduced intake contribute to hypoglycemia.  Liver injury causes elevated transaminases, hepatomegaly, and jaundice; renal tubular dysfunction can cause metabolic acidosis.  Excess galactose is also converted to galactitol, which accumulates in the lens and causes cataracts.  In addition, affected infants are predisposed to Escherichia colisepsis (eg, leukocytosis with a left shift, gram-negative bacteremia), possibly due in part to impaired neutrophil bacterial killing caused by elevated galactose levels.

Treatment involves restricting dietary galactose by replacing breast milk with an appropriate lactose-free formula, such as a soy-based infant formula.  Dietary restriction typically improves the acute hepatic and renal manifestations; concurrent sepsis requires antibiotic treatment.

(Choice A)  Intestinal lactase hydrolyzes lactose to glucose and galactose.  Lactase deficiency causes lactose malabsorption with bloating and osmotic diarrhea; it does not cause the characteristic liver injury seen in this patient.  Furthermore, congenital lactase deficiency is rare.

(Choice B)  Aldose reductase converts galactose to galactitol, which contributes to cataract formation in galactosemia.  Deficiency of this enzyme would not block the main pathway of galactose metabolism.

(Choice C)  Galactokinase deficiency is a less common, milder form of galactosemia characterized by cataract formation due to galactitol accumulation in the lens.  Because galactose-1-phosphate does not accumulate, affected infants are typically well-appearing and lack the hepatic and renal dysfunction seen in classic galactosemia.

(Choice E)  Phosphoglucomutase interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking glycogen metabolism with glycolysis.  Its deficiency can cause hypoglycemia and muscle dysfunction but is not associated with the characteristic susceptibility to E coli sepsis.

Educational objective:Classic galactosemia is caused by galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase deficiency and presents shortly after milk feeding begins with vomiting, hypoglycemia, liver dysfunction, and susceptibility to Escherichia coli sepsis.  Treatment requires dietary galactose restriction, including replacement of breast milk with an appropriate lactose-free formula.​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​
